abstract: Background Bronchial asthma is a heterogeneous inflammatory airway disease with complex etiology. While the respiratory microbiome and host metabolism are implicated, their integrated roles in defining asthma subtypes remain underexplored. Methods This multi-omics study utilized 16S rRNA sequencing and untargeted metabolomics on sputum samples from asthma patients and healthy controls. We characterized airway microbial and metabolic profiles, identified asthma subgroups through unsupervised clustering, and investigated microbe-metabolite interactions. Results Asthma patients exhibited typical clinical hallmarks including elevated IgE and impaired lung function. Microbiome analysis revealed significant enrichment of Streptococcus , Veillonella , and Prevotella as key asthma-associated taxa, alongside dysregulation of crucial lipid metabolic pathways (eg, alpha-linolenic and arachidonic acid). Four highly discriminative diagnostic biomarkers (AUC >0.9), including cis -aconitic acid and LPE 20:1, were identified, indicating specific metabolic perturbations. Unsupervised clustering stratified asthma patients into 2 distinct endotypes: a severe Streptococcus -dominant cluster (Cluster 1) with profound systemic and local metabolic disturbances, and a milder cluster (Cluster 2) with microbial and metabolic profiles resembling healthy controls. These endotypes displayed differential lipid and amino acid metabolism, suggesting unique underlying mechanisms. Conclusion Our findings precisely delineate asthma endotypes driven by distinct microbiome-metabolome interactions, providing novel diagnostic biomarkers and pathway-specific therapeutic targets. This study critically advances our understanding of asthma heterogeneity, highlighting the importance of integrated multi-omics for personalized precision medicine strategies. Clinical trial number Not applicable.

Study population
Patients with diagnosed asthma were recruited from the First Affiliated Hospital of Guangzhou Medical University between April 2024 and December 2024. Asthma diagnosis followed the Global Initiative for Asthma (GINA) guidelines,

bronchodilator reversibility of more than 200 mL and FEV
1
percentage change of at least 12%; or methacholine challenge of less than 8 mg/mL; or peak flow rate (PEF) diurnal variation; or variable FEV
1
/FVC ratio.
Eligible participants also met the following study inclusion criteria: (1) Aged between 18 and 70 years; (2) No history of smoking; (3) Underwent baseline assessments prior to enrollment, including pulmonary function, asthma symptoms, and asthma-specific quality of life; (4) Initially diagnosed with mild-to-moderate asthma exacerbation or persistent asthma according to the American Thoracic Society guidelines and GINA guidelines; and (5) Routinely treated with an equivalent dose of inhaled corticosteroids for over 6 months but experienced more than 1 acute exacerbation in the past 6 months.
Exclusion criteria:
History of chronic lung diseases or any other diagnosed conditions, ongoing immunotherapy, malignancy diagnosis, current/recent ex-smokers (<1 year), recent respiratory infection, or antibiotic use in past 4 weeks.
Samples collection
Sputum induction involved isotonic saline with a bronchodilator, processed as in Ref.
22
. ICS or other inhaled corticosteroids were stopped for 24 h. Samples with >10% squamous cells were excluded. Precipitates were used for microbiome analysis, supernatants stored at −80 °C for metabolism analysis. All participants underwent spirometry per ERS guidelines to assess lung function and airway obstruction severity.
Ethical approval was obtained from the Ethics Committee of The First Affiliated Hospital of Guangzhou Medical University, with approval codes 2022 No.121 and 2024 No. G-007. Written informed consent was obtained from all participants prior to inclusion in the study. This study was conducted in accordance with the ethical principles of the Declaration of Helsinki.
16S rRNA amplicon sequencing
Microbial DNA from sputum was extracted using the FastDNA Spin Kit and purity was checked with a Nanodrop. Integrity was assessed via agarose gel electrophoresis. PCR amplified the V3–V4 regions of the 16S rRNA gene according to universal primers (515F: 5′-GGACTACHVGGGTWTCTAAT-3′, 806R: 5′- GGACTACHVGGGTWTCTAAT- 3′). PCR products were purified, quantified, and sequenced on an Illumina NovaSeq6000 at the Novogene Bioinformatics Technology Co., Ltd. The paired-end reads were assigned using barcode and then were merged with FLASH (Fast Length Adjustment of SHort reads) (V1.2.11) software.
23
High-quality filtering of the raw tags was performed to obtain clean tags using QIIME (Quantitative Insights into Microbial Ecology) (Version QIIME2-202202). After that, chimeric sequences were compared with Silva Database and using the UCHIME algorithm to detect and remove chimera sequences. A final effective sequence analysis was performed using Uparse software (Uparse V7.0.1001).
Microbiomics study
Sequences with a similarity index greater than 97% were assigned to the same operational taxonomic units (OTUs). Alpha diversity metrics (Chao1, Shannon Diversity, Simpson, and Richness indice) were calculated for the OTU table using alpha rarefaction. The beta diversity metric was calculated on the OTU table and visualized using principal coordinate analysis (PCoA) and non-metric multidimensional scaling (NMDS) analysis. The alpha diversity and beta diversity analysis were calculated with QIIME software (version 1.9.1) and displayed with R software (version 2.15.3). ANOSIM analysis was performed to evaluate the statistical significance of microbial community structure differences between groups. Linear discriminant analysis Effect Size (LEfSe) was employed to identify statistically significant (Kruskal-Wallis test,
p
< 0.05; LDA score >4.0) and biologically relevant taxonomic differences between groups.
Non-targeted metabolomics profiling
Metabolites were extracted from sputum and tested with a liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS). The metabolomics analysis was performed using a Vanquish UHPLC system (ThermoFisher, Germany) in Novogene Co., Ltd. (Beijing, China). Samples were injected onto a Hypersil Goldcolumn (100 × 2.1 mm, 1.9 μm) using a 12-min linear gradient at a flow rate of 0.2 mL/min. The eluents for the positive and negative polarity modes were eluent A (0.1% FA in Water) and eluent B (Methanol). The solvent gradient was set as follows: 2% B, 1.5 min; 2–85% B, 3 min; 85–100% B, 10 min; 100-2% B, 10.1 min; 2% B, 12 min. Q ExactiveTM HF mass spectrometer was operated in positive/negative polarity mode with spray voltage of 3.5 kV, capillary temperature of 320 °C, sheath gas flow rate of 35 psi and aux gas flow rate of 10 L/min, S-lens RF level of 60, Aux gas heater temperature of 350 °C. The raw data files generated by UHPLC-MS/MS were processed using the Compound Discoverer 3.3 (CD3.3, ThermoFisher) to perform peak alignment, peak picking, and quantitation for each metabolite.
Metabolomics study
Orthogonal partial least squares-discriminant analysis (OPLS-DA) were used to explore whether all samples can be significantly clustered in different groups. We applied univariate analysis (
t
-test) to calculate the statistical significance (
P
-value). Volcano plots were used to filter metabolites of interest which based on log2 (Fold Change), and -log10(
P
-value) of metabolites by ggplot2 in R language
P
-value <0.05 was considered as statistically significant and correlation plots were ploted by corrplot package in R language. The functions of these metabolites and metabolic pathways were studied using the KEGG database. The potential biomarkers were screened through MetaboAnalyst 4.0 (
http://www.metaboanalyst.ca/
) for potential metabolic pathways, with the impact values above 0.10 and p values below 0.05. To evaluate the discriminatory power of classifiers in distinguishing between healthy controls and patients, the Receiver Operating Characteristic (ROC) Curve was employed. Based on the differential metabolites obtained by the above analysis, ROC analysis was used to obtain curve and calculate the area under the curve (AUC), providing a quantitative measure of the model's performance. Furthermore, we ventured to enhance the predictive capability of our model by integrating the identified biomarkers.
Statistical analysis
Continuous variables were expressed as mean ± standard deviation (SD) for normally distributed data or as median with interquartile range (IQR) for non-normally distributed data. Normality was assessed using the Shapiro-Wilk test. Between-group comparisons were conducted using independent t-tests for normally distributed variables and Wilcoxon rank-sum tests for non-normally distributed variables. Categorical variables were analyzed using the chi-square test or Fisher's exact test, as appropriate. All statistical analysis about the identification of distinct metabolites was completed with R (v4.0.2) basic statistical packages.

Introduction
Bronchial asthma is a chronic inflammatory disorder of the airways characterized by recurrent episodes of wheezing, breathlessness, chest tightness, and coughing.
1
It affects a significant proportion of the global population, with a substantial burden on both individuals and healthcare systems.
2
Despite advances in understanding and managing asthma, the disease remains heterogeneous, with varying clinical presentations, responses to treatment, and underlying pathophysiological mechanisms.
3
This heterogeneity poses challenges in diagnosis, prognosis, and personalized treatment strategies.
4
Recent studies have highlighted the role of the airway microbiome in the pathogenesis of asthma. The lung, once considered a sterile environment, is now recognized to harbor a diverse microbial community that interacts dynamically with the host immune system.
5
Alterations in the composition and function of the airway microbiome have been implicated in asthma exacerbations, disease severity, and response to therapy.
6
For instance, some studies have revealed characteristic features in the airway microbiota of asthma patients, including an enrichment of
Proteobacteria
and a reduction in
Firmicutes
,
7
specific bacterial taxa, such as
Streptococcus
and
Haemophilus
, have been associated with asthma severity and inflammation.
8
However, the precise mechanisms by which the microbiome influences asthma pathogenesis remain incompletely understood.
Metabolomics, the study of small molecules or metabolites within biological systems, offers insights into the biochemical processes underlying diseases. In asthma, metabolomic profiling has revealed alterations in pathways related to lipid metabolism, inflammation, and oxidative stress.
9
These metabolic changes may reflect the interplay between the airway microbiome and host immune responses.
10
Metabolomic research has further reported abnormalities in arachidonic acid and linoleic acid metabolism in asthma, providing potential biomarkers for disease diagnosis, subtyping, and therapeutic monitoring.
11
,
12
However, metabolomic analyses have primarily relied on systemic biofluids such as blood and urine, failing to capture the localized metabolic milieu of the respiratory tract.
13
Further constraints include small cohort sizes and insufficient adjustment for confounding factors, particularly corticosteroid therapy.
14
Moreover, the majority of investigations have employed single-omics methodologies, neglecting the potential synergies between microbial composition and host metabolism. Addressing these limitations through integrated multi-omics approaches will be essential for elucidating the complex host-microbe dynamics underlying asthma pathogenesis.
Despite these advances, several gaps remain in our understanding of asthma pathogenesis. The disease presents with varying clinical phenotypes, ranging from mild, stable disease to rapidly progressive forms characterized by frequent exacerbations and significant comorbidities,
15
Mild asthma patients experience relatively mild symptoms, which only manifest upon exposure to specific allergens or after strenuous exercise.
16
For patients with moderate asthma, symptom severity increases, requiring regular use of low-to medium-dose inhaled corticosteroids.
17
,
18
Severe asthma patients suffer from frequent and severe symptoms that significantly impact daily life and work and lead to a severe decline in lung function.
19
This heterogeneity is likely driven by complex interactions between genetic, environmental, and microbial factors.
20
For instance, different asthma endotypes may exhibit distinct microbial and metabolic profiles. The heterogeneity of asthma complicates the identification of consistent microbial and metabolic signatures across patient populations. To bridge these gaps, it is imperative to adopt integrated approaches that merge microbiome and metabolome analyses with in-depth clinical profiling of asthma patients across different subtypes.
In this study, we hypothesized that the airway microbiome and metabolome differ between asthma patients and healthy controls and that these differences may contribute to the heterogeneity of asthma. We employed a multi-omics approach that integrates 16S rRNA gene sequencing and metabolomics. Our study aimed to characterize the airway microbiome and metabolome in bronchial asthma patients in comparison to healthy controls, identify asthma subtypes based on microbial community composition and subsequently compare their clinical and metabolic features, and explore the relationships between specific microbial taxa and metabolic pathways involved in asthma pathogenesis. Through these efforts, we aspire to gain novel insights into the mechanisms driving asthma heterogeneity and to uncover potential biomarkers and therapeutic targets that could pave the way for personalized asthma management strategies.

Microbiota in the respiratory tract of asthma patients versus HCs
Analysis of the structure of microbial communities
To investigate these dynamics, 16S rRNA amplicon sequencing of sputum samples was performed to explore shifts in lung microbiota and uncover alterations in the structure and function of the lower respiratory tract microbiota. Based on Usearch statistics, raw 16S rRNA sequencing data using primers 515F and 806R were filtered using QIIME software, followed by sequence splicing with FLASH software to generate tag sequences. A total of 56 high-quality samples were obtained from sputum sequencing, with an average of 87,495 valid sequences per sample. At a 97% similarity threshold, 2696 Operational Taxonomic Units (OTUs) were identified.
Our alpha-diversity analysis demonstrated consistent within-group microbial diversity across all study cohorts, Metrics such as Chao1, Shannon Diversity, Simpson, and Richness indices reveal significant differences in species richness or diversity (
p
< 0.05) (
Fig. 1
a–d). In contrast, beta-diversity metrics revealed significant compositional differences between HC and AS, with both PCoA (R

Fig. 1

Fig. 1
g), suggesting that while specific taxa may vary, the overall architectural organization of microbial communities remains statistically indistinguishable.

We performed hierarchical clustering of all asthma samples using Jaccard distances and Ward's linkage method. This data-driven approach revealed 2 distinct asthma subtypes, enabling more precise characterization of microbiome variations associated with asthma endotypes. Discussion
Our study employed a dual-omics approach combining 16S rRNA sequencing and mass spectrometry-based metabolomics to investigate airway microbiome and metabolic profiles in asthma. The analysis revealed significant microbial shifts, with asthma patients showing increased abundances of
Streptococcus
and
Veillonella
, while healthy controls exhibited greater prevalence of
Xanthomonadaceae
and
Stenotrophomonas
, along with distinct metabolic disturbances in lipid and oxidative stress pathways.
To contextualize our findings within the broader landscape of asthma research, we compared our results with those of large-scale multi-omics studies, such as the U-BIOPRED consortium, which serves as an international benchmark for the molecular characterization of asthma. U-BIOPRED integrated 6 omics data blocks (microarray transcriptomics, gene set variation analysis, SomaSCAN proteomics, shotgun proteomics, 16S microbiome sequencing, and shotgun metagenomic sequencing) from induced sputum,
24
identifying 5 stable omics-associated clusters (OACs). Their findings highlighted distinct endotypes, such as OAC3 with predominant eosinophilia and OAC2 with neutrophilia and microbial dysbiosis involving
Moraxella catarrhalis
and
Haemophilus influenzae
. Additionally, another U-BIOPRED study conducted transcriptomic analysis of blood, bronchial and nasal epithelial brushings, bronchial biopsies, and sputum cells from frequent exacerbators (FE) and persistent frequent exacerbators (PFE), linking FE and PFE to poor asthma control, higher type 1 and type 2 pathway activation, and the differentially expressed transcript CEACAM5 in bronchial biopsies.
25
In contrast, our study employed a dual-omics approach, combining 16S rRNA sequencing and metabolomics in a smaller, clinically well-characterized cohort, focusing on airway-specific microbiome-metabolite interactions. Unlike U-BIOPRED's comprehensive multi-omics profiling, our targeted analysis revealed specific correlations, such as Streptococcus with immunomodulatory metabolites (eg, Tacrolimus) and
Stenotrophomonas
with anti-inflammatory metabolites (eg, 12(S)-HETE), complementing U-BIOPRED by elucidating lipid and oxidative stress pathways linked to microbial dysbiosis. Our focus on airway samples enabled refined examination of local dynamics, highlighting novel taxon-specific interactions and potential therapeutic targets, such as lipid-based biomarkers, not emphasized in U-BIOPRED.
Unsupervised clustering identified 2 asthma endotypes, Cluster 1 characterized by
Streptococcus
-dominant dysbiosis, impaired lung function, elevated IgE levels, and disrupted homeostasis of both lipids and caffeine, tryptophan metabolism. Cluster 2 maintains a homeostatic microbiome profile similar to the healthy baseline. Notably, taxon-specific metabolic correlations were observed:
Stenotrophomonas
abundance inversely correlated with anti-inflammatory metabolites, while
Streptococcus
showed positive associations with immunomodulators. These findings provide novel insights into microbial contributions to asthma pathogenesis and establish a microbiome-metabolite interaction framework for developing precision management strategies.
Unveiling key differential features of airway microbiome and metabolome profiles in asthma patients compared to healthy controls
In our comparative analysis of airway microbiome and metabolome profiles between asthma patients and healthy controls, several key differential features were unveiled. At the phylum level, although the overall microbial structure showed some similarities, significant differences emerged at the family and genus levels. For instance, the asthma group exhibited an enrichment of
Streptococcus
and
Veillonella
compared to the healthy controls, whereas
Xanthomonadaceae
and
Stenotrophomonas
were more prevalent in the latter. These findings are in line with previous studies that have highlighted the role of specific microbial taxa in asthma pathogenesis.
26
The enrichment of certain bacteria in asthma patients may contribute to the dysregulation of the immune system, leading to airway inflammation and hyperresponsiveness.
Metabolomically, we observed distinct patterns between the 2 groups. Asthma patients showed significant metabolic perturbations, particularly in pathways related to lipid metabolism, inflammation, and oxidative stress. Four biomarkers originating from different metabolic pathways suggest that bronchial asthma is not caused by the abnormality of a single metabolic pathway. For instance, lipid metabolism abnormalities (LPE 20:1) may affect the structure and function of cell membranes,
27
thereby influencing the normal physiological activities of airway epithelial cells.
28
Nucleic acid metabolism abnormalities (dihydrothymine) may be related to cellular processes such as proliferation and differentiation, impacting the development and function of immune cells.
29
Abnormalities in the tricarboxylic acid cycle involving cis-Aconitic acid may affect cellular energy metabolism,
30
leading to abnormal energy supply and accumulation of metabolic products in airway inflammatory cells.
31
,
32
Moreover, abnormalities in organic compounds with specific aromatic ring structures may reflect changes in oxidative stress or certain specific biochemical reactions within the body.
33
These findings contribute to a deeper understanding of the pathogenesis of bronchial asthma and provide clues for identifying new therapeutic targets.
Integrating microbiome and metabolome data enabled a more holistic comprehension of the disparities between asthma patients and healthy individuals. We observed that the
Stenotrophomonas
genus negatively correlated with nearly all the metabolites, The negative correlation between the
Streptococcus
genus and 2-Methoxyestrone, coupled with its positive correlation with other metabolites, suggests a complex regulatory function. It is likely that
Streptococcus
selectively modulates certain metabolic pathways, with 2-Methoxyestrone potentially being a crucial target or a by-product of a pathway affected by this genus.
34
Furthermore, the positive correlation of
Lactobacillales
with nearly all metabolites highlights its capacity to foster a diverse and metabolically active environment. This order may enhance metabolic processes, resulting in an elevated abundance of various metabolites.
35
Identification of distinct asthma subtypes based on microbiome - metabolome correlations: Insights into asthma heterogeneity
The hierarchical clustering of asthma samples based on Jaccard distances and Ward's linkage method successfully revealed 2 distinct asthma subgroups. Cluster 1 exhibited marked physiological impairments, characterized by significantly lower lung function parameters (FEV1/FVC ratio, FEV1, and FVC) compared to Cluster 2. Additionally, Cluster 1 had significantly elevated IgE levels, suggesting a more severe allergic component in this subgroup. These findings are consistent with previous studies that have linked reduced lung function and elevated IgE levels to increased asthma severity and poor prognosis.
36
However, it is important to note that the classification of "severe" and "mild" in this study is based specifically on the data-driven clustering model utilizing IgE and lung function parameters, and does not represent a comprehensive clinical severity assessment as defined by contemporary asthma guidelines, which incorporate additional dimensions such as symptom control, exacerbation frequency, and oral corticosteroid use. The distinct clinical profile of Cluster 1 indicates that it may represent a more severe asthma endotype within our analytical framework, which may require targeted therapeutic approaches to control symptoms and prevent disease progression. Future studies with larger cohorts are needed to validate these clusters using guideline-recommended parameters, including disease activity scores and T2 inflammation biomarkers such as FeNO, to establish their full clinical relevance.
Microbial diversity analysis further supported the differentiation of the 2 asthma subtypes. Although Cluster 1 had a high microbial diversity, it presented an immune imbalance characterized by elevated IgE levels. The microbial composition of Cluster 2 shows significant similarity to that of healthy controls. This is in line with some previous studies.
37
In contrast to Cluster 2, Cluster 1 has a higher diversity of the respiratory microbiome, which is somewhat contrary to our initial expectations. It is generally believed that a decrease in microbiome diversity may be associated with the onset and progression of diseases, as reduced diversity could lead to incomplete functions and ecological imbalance of the microbial community. However, in this study, despite its high microbiome diversity, Cluster 1 presents an immune imbalance characterized by elevated Ig E levels. This suggests that microbiome diversity is not the sole determinant of immune balance, and that the types, relative abundances, and interactions among microorganisms may be more crucial.
38
It is possible that specific microorganisms or microbial combinations within the high - diversity microbiome interact with the host immune system in a way that leads to immune imbalance.
Metabolomics analysis has unveiled unique metabolic characteristics between the 2 asthma subtypes. By employing rigorous criteria, we identified 20 differential metabolites that can significantly distinguish asthma patients in Cluster 1 from those in Cluster 2. Pathway analysis revealed significant changes in several metabolic pathways, including caffeine metabolism, fatty acid degradation, pyrimidine metabolism, and tryptophan metabolism. This finding is in harmony with the results of certain prior metabolomics research, as those studies have also uncovered abnormal fatty acid metabolism in asthma patients,
39
paralleling the alterations in the fatty acid degradation pathway that we observed in our investigation.
In addition, the 4 lipid-based biomarkers we identified (LPE O-16:1, LPE O-18:2, LPE O-20:3, and LPE O-20:1) exhibit excellent diagnostic performance for Cluster 1 asthma. This aligns with the potential roles of lipids in asthma diagnosis and prognosis assessment found in some studies.
40
Lipids play crucial roles in processes such as cell signaling and inflammatory responses.
41
The alterations in lipid metabolism in asthma patients may reflect the pathophysiological processes of the disease.
We calculated the Spearman's correlation between differential taxa and 20 differential metabolites identified in the comparison between these 2 clusters. We observed that the
Stenotrophomonas
genus exhibited a negative correlation with 12(S)-HETE and N1-cyclohexyl-4-(4-fluorobenzyl)-1,4 - diazepane-1-carbothioamide. 12(S)-HETE is an anti-inflammatory metabolite,
42
and the negative correlation suggests that the presence or abundance of
Stenotrophomonas
may be associated with a reduction in the levels of this beneficial metabolite. On the other hand,
Streptococcus
showed a positive correlation with Tacrolimus, Palmitooylcarn, and 12(S)-HETE. Tacrolimus is an immunomodulatory compound,
43
and the positive correlation between
Streptococcus
and tacrolimus implies a potential role of this bacterial genus in modulating the immune response through its association with this compound. The observed associations between
Stenotrophomonas
and anti - inflammatory metabolites, as well as between Streptococcus and immunomodulatory compounds, highlight potential mechanistic differences between the 2 asthma clusters. These differences are crucial as they may contribute to the varying clinical manifestations, disease severity, and treatment responses observed in asthma patients. Further functional validation studies are warranted to elucidate the exact mechanisms by which these microbial taxa influence metabolic pathways and immune responses in asthma.
Implications and future directions
The identification of distinct asthma subtypes with unique clinical, microbiological, and metabolomic profiles has important implications for asthma management. Personalized medicine approaches that take into account the heterogeneity of asthma may lead to more effective treatment strategies. For example, patients in Cluster 1, who represent a more severe asthma endotype, may benefit from more aggressive anti-inflammatory therapies and targeted microbiome modulation.
However, it is important to acknowledge the limitations of this study. The relatively small sample size, particularly after subdivision into clusters, may affect the stability of the unsupervised clustering model and increases the risk of overfitting in our statistical analyses. Furthermore, the single-center and relatively homogeneous nature of our cohort limits the generalizability of our findings. While our findings provide compelling exploratory evidence for the existence of these endotypes, they require validation in larger, independent, multicenter cohorts. Future studies with expanded sample sizes from diverse geographical locations are essential to confirm the robustness and generalizability of our results, and to further refine the clinical and biological characteristics of these proposed asthma subtypes.
Future studies should focus on validating the diagnostic and prognostic value of the identified biomarkers in larger cohorts of asthma patients. Additionally, functional studies are needed to elucidate the mechanisms underlying the microbiome-metabolite interactions and their role in asthma pathogenesis. Longitudinal studies can also help to determine how microbial communities and metabolic profiles change over time and how these changes are associated with disease progression and response to treatment.
Conclusion
In conclusion, this study utilized a dual - omics approach to compare the airway microbiome and metabolome of asthma patients and healthy controls, asthma patients showing increased abundances of
Streptococcus
and
Veillonella
, while healthy controls exhibited greater prevalence of
Xanthomonadaceae
and
Stenotrophomonas
, along with distinct metabolic disturbances in lipid and oxidative stress pathways. Additionally, 4 highly accurate diagnostic biomarkers were discovered. Furthermore, our multi-omics study uncovered distinct microbiome-metabolome signatures that redefine asthma heterogeneity. We identified 2 clinically relevant endotypes - a severe
Streptococcus
-dominant cluster with characteristic metabolic disturbances and a milder cluster resembling healthy controls. The discovery of robust diagnostic biomarkers (AUC>0.9) and specific microbe-metabolite interactions, particularly the immunomodulatory role of
Streptococcus
and anti-inflammatory associations of
Stenotrophomonas
, provides a new paradigm for understanding asthma pathogenesis. These findings not only advance our knowledge of airway microbial ecology but also lay the foundation for developing precision diagnostic tools and targeted therapies based on individual microbiome-metabolic profiles.
